content.title: About
content.content: Cheese pastry puffs are light, airy pastries made from dough enriched with creamy cheese. They have a golden crust and a soft, cheesy interior, often served as a snack or dessert.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheese puffs are popular in European cuisine, especially in Germany and Austria.
The dough is usually made from wheat flour, butter and eggs, while the filling contains cottage or cream cheese.
Puffs can be sweet (with sugar and vanilla) or savory (with herbs and spices).
Traditionally they are deep‑fried, but modern recipes bake them to reduce fat.
They are often served with sour cream dip or a fruit coulis.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The cheese provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Cream cheese is rich in calcium, supporting bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the dough and cheese contain B2 and B12 vitamins important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low sugar (in savory versions)
items.content: Savory cheese puffs can be a lower‑sugar alternative to sweet pastries when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Dietary fiber (when whole‑grain flour is used)
items.content: Using whole‑grain flour adds fiber, which aids digestion.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese puffs may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Traditional deep‑fried puffs are calorie‑dense and contain saturated fats.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Savory versions can be high in salt, which is a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Standard dough contains wheat, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cheese puffs warm; they can be eaten as a snack, added to salads, or paired with dips such as sour cream, garlic sauce, or fruit coulis.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep puffs in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze for up to 2 months.

chicken-breast-baked-or-broiled-skin-eat.title: Chicken breast, baked or broiled, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is a lean cut of poultry meat, rich in protein and low in fat. In this product the breast is pre‑cooked (baked or broiled) and served with the skin, which keeps it juicy and adds flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast is the most popular protein source in many countries.
Baking or broiling with the skin helps retain more B‑vitamins.
The skin provides beneficial monounsaturated fats and collagen.
Pre‑cooked breast is convenient for storage and quick reheating.
In the United States chicken breast is a staple of many diet plans because of its low calorie density.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 31 g of complete protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: When cooked without added oil, the breast remains low‑fat, supporting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B3 (niacin) and B6 aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: phosphorus and selenium
items.content: Phosphorus contributes to bone health, while selenium offers antioxidant protection.

items.title: Collagen from the skin
items.content: The skin contains collagen, which supports skin, hair and joint health.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient reheating can allow bacteria such as Salmonella to grow.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content in processed versions
items.content: Some pre‑cooked products contain added salt; individuals with hypertension should check labels.

items.title: Fat in the skin
items.content: While flavorful, the skin adds extra calories and saturated fat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat the chicken breast in the microwave, on a skillet, or in the oven. Slice it for salads, sandwiches, add to pasta, or use in quick‑prep meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked breast in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for 2‑3 months. Heat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken feet are edible parts of a chicken consisting of bone, skin, and a small amount of meat. They are popular in Asian cuisines, especially in China, Vietnam, and the Philippines, where they are often boiled, fried, or braised in sauces. The feet have a gelatinous texture and a rich flavor that readily absorbs aromatic spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken feet are frequently used in stocks because they add body and flavor.
In China, chicken feet are considered a delicacy and are served as bar snacks and in restaurants.
Traditionally they are cooked in soy sauce with ginger, garlic, and spices, or in sweet‑sour sauces.
In many cultures the feet are valued for their collagen content, which is thought to benefit skin and joints.
Chicken feet can be frozen and stored for up to 12 months without loss of quality.

items.title: Rich in collagen
items.content: The skin and cartilage of chicken feet provide collagen, which supports skin elasticity, hair health, and joint function.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Although the meat amount is modest, chicken feet still deliver complete protein needed for tissue repair and growth.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Feet are a good source of calcium, phosphorus, and magnesium, important for bone health and nerve function.

items.title: Low in fat when prepared properly
items.content: Steaming or boiling chicken feet keeps the fat content low compared with deep‑fried preparations.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: They contain glucosamine and chondroitin, which may help maintain a healthy immune response.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken products, including feet.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improperly handled feet can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; thorough cooking is essential.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: When marinated or cooked in soy sauce, the sodium level can become excessive.

items.title: Chewing hazards
items.content: Bones can be very hard; cooking until tender reduces the risk of oral injury.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Feet are usually boiled until tender, then stir‑fried in sauce, baked, or added to soups. They can be served as a snack, tossed into rice dishes, noodles, or salads. Often the skin is scorched and peeled before cooking to improve texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh chicken feet in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen feet can be stored in an airtight bag in the freezer for up to 12 months. Before cooking, check for an off‑odor; a sour or rancid smell indicates spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Coconut is the fruit of the coconut palm (Cocos nucifera), cultivated in tropical regions worldwide. The packaged product contains whole coconuts that have been stripped of the outer fibrous husk but retain the inner flesh and coconut water. The nuts have a distinctive aroma, a mildly sweet taste, and a dense yet tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The coconut palm is often called the “tree of life” in many tropical cultures.
Coconut water is a natural isotonic drink rich in electrolytes.
Coconut flesh contains about 30 % saturated fat, mainly lauric acid.
Coconut oil is extracted from dried flesh (copra) by cold pressing.
Whole coconuts can float in water for up to nine days thanks to their hollow interior.

items.title: Rich in electrolytes
items.content: Coconut water provides potassium, sodium, magnesium, and calcium, helping maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Source of lauric acid
items.content: Lauric acid exhibits antibacterial and antiviral properties.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Compounds from coconut flesh may help lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Antioxidant effect
items.content: Coconut contains phenolic compounds that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The fiber in the flesh promotes intestinal motility and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to coconut products.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive consumption of coconut flesh or oil can increase overall saturated fat intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Coconut flesh and oil are energy‑dense; portion sizes should be moderated.

items.title: Copper content
items.content: Large amounts of coconut may lead to excess copper in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Packaged coconut can be eaten fresh as a snack, added to smoothies, yogurt, salads, or baked goods. The flesh is cut into cubes, and the coconut water is enjoyed chilled or used as a base for sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole coconuts in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep the flesh in an airtight container in the refrigerator and consume within 3–5 days. Coconut water should be refrigerated and used within 2 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Dandelion greens (Taraxacum officinale) are the edible young leaves of this perennial herb that grows in temperate regions worldwide. Raw leaves have a mildly bitter, refreshing flavor and a crisp texture. They are used in salads, smoothies, juices, and as a garnish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The leaves are rich in vitamins A, C, and K, as well as minerals such as calcium, iron, and potassium.
In traditional medicine dandelion has been used to support liver and bile function.
All parts of the plant—from root to flower—are edible, but the young leaves are considered the most tender and flavorful.
Dandelions emerge early in spring when the soil is still cool, making them one of the first available greens.
In some cultures dandelion leaves symbolize purity and renewal.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: The greens contain beta‑carotene, vitamin C, and polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber in the leaves promotes regular bowel movements and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory properties
items.content: Phytochemicals such as quercetin have demonstrated anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Vitamin K and calcium contribute to bone mineralization.

items.title: Liver support
items.content: Bitter compounds (taraxinic acid) stimulate bile production, aiding liver function.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to dandelion.

items.title: Pesticide residue
items.content: If harvested near roads or treated fields, leaves may contain contaminants; prefer gathering from clean, organic sites.

items.title: Thyroid concerns
items.content: Large amounts can affect thyroid function due to goitrogenic substances.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw greens can be tossed into salads, blended into smoothies or juices, or used as a garnish for meat dishes. Lightly blanching in boiling water reduces bitterness, then shock in ice water. Young leaves are milder, while older leaves become more bitter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the greens in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–5 days. Rinse and thoroughly dry them before storage to prevent spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Salmon is a fatty fish from the family Salmonidae, found in the North Atlantic and North Pacific oceans and in freshwater rivers where it spawns. It has pink to orange-red flesh and a rich, mild flavor. Salmon is eaten fresh, smoked, cured, canned, or cooked in many ways and is widely known for its omega-3 content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salmon are anadromous: they are born in freshwater, live in the ocean, and return to rivers to spawn.
There is one Atlantic salmon species and several Pacific species, including sockeye, coho, chinook, pink, and chum.
The pink-orange color comes from astaxanthin, a pigment from the crustaceans and krill salmon eat.
Salmon sold today is either wild-caught or farmed.
Salmon is one of the best-known sources of omega-3 fatty acids among foods.

items.title: Rich in omega-3 fatty acids
items.content: Salmon is a good source of EPA and DHA, which support normal heart and brain function.

items.title: Source of high-quality protein
items.content: Salmon provides complete protein for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Provides vitamin D
items.content: Salmon is one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12 and selenium
items.content: These nutrients support red blood cell formation, nervous system function, and immune health.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Fish allergy can be serious and is lifelong for many people.

items.title: Raw or undercooked fish
items.content: Raw or undercooked salmon may carry parasites and bacteria and is not recommended for pregnant women, young children, or people with weakened immunity.

items.title: Contaminants
items.content: Salmon can contain small amounts of environmental contaminants. Follow local guidance on how often to eat it, especially during pregnancy.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: High doses of omega-3 supplements may affect blood clotting. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Salmon can be baked, grilled, pan-seared, poached, or steamed. Smoked or cured salmon is often eaten on bread or in salads, and canned salmon can be used in sandwiches, patties, and pasta. Cook fresh salmon until it flakes easily with a fork.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh salmon in the coldest part of the refrigerator and cook it within one to two days. For longer storage, wrap it tightly and freeze it, then thaw it in the refrigerator. Cooked salmon should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within about three days. Follow the label for smoked and canned salmon.

content.title: About
content.content: Snow peas (Pisum sativum) are young pea pods eaten fresh, usually after a brief cooking step without added fat. They are crisp, mildly sweet, and rich in vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Snow peas belong to the legume family and are the ancestors of larger pea varieties.
Both the pod and the seeds are edible, unlike many other peas.
They are grown in temperate climates and are a staple in Asian cuisine.
Snow peas are low‑calorie – about 42 kcal per 100 g.
They can be eaten raw, but are often blanched briefly to retain bright color and crunch.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes snow peas suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes, including snow peas.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Raw pods can contain small amounts of toxic compounds; a short heat treatment is recommended.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes may cause increased gas in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Snow peas can be eaten raw in salads, quickly steamed or boiled for 2–3 minutes, added to stir‑fries, soups, and pasta dishes. When cooking without added fat, steaming or blanching works best.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh snow peas in the refrigerator in a sealed bag or container for up to 5 days. Frozen peas retain quality for up to 8 months.
